newInput: Can you explain how garbage collection works in Go?

answersA.title: Garbage collection in Go
answersA.text: Garbage collection in Go is a concurrent, tri-color, mark-and-sweep system. It works by identifying and reclaiming memory that is no longer in use by the program. The process involves marking all reachable objects and then sweeping away the unmarked ones. This happens concurrently with the application, minimizing pauses.

answersA.text: Kotlin coroutines are a way to write asynchronous code that looks sequential. They are lighter than threads, allowing for many more concurrent operations with less overhead. Threads are managed by the operating system and have a heavier context-switching cost. Coroutines are cooperative, meaning they yield control explicitly, while threads are preemptive.

answersA.title: Kotlin coroutines vs threads
answersA.text: Kotlin coroutines are a more lightweight concurrency primitive than threads. Threads are managed by the operating system and have significant overhead in terms of memory and context switching. Coroutines, on the other hand, are managed by the Kotlin runtime and allow for cooperative multitasking, meaning they yield control voluntarily. This makes them much more efficient for handling a large number of concurrent operations.

answersA.title: Kotlin coroutines vs threads
answersA.text: Kotlin coroutines are a way to write asynchronous code that is more sequential and easier to read than traditional callback-based approaches. They are a lightweight abstraction over threads, meaning many coroutines can run on a single thread. Threads, on the other hand, are a more heavyweight operating system construct. Coroutines are managed by the Kotlin runtime and can be suspended and resumed without blocking the underlying thread, whereas threads typically block when waiting for an operation to complete.
